title: My lesson observation + coaching template
author: Craig Barton
summary: Barton shares the seven-part template he now uses to observe lessons and run coaching conversations, built on ideas from Adam Boxer, Ollie Lovell and Josh Goodrich after years of giving vague, unactionable feedback. The sections run from context and lesson commentary through specific praise to prompt, a testable hypothesis, critical evidence, diagnostic questions and a suggested action. A worked example follows a Year 9 Do Now in which he hypothesised that asking for three simultaneous answers on mini-whiteboards would hide wrong answers, and objective photographic evidence convinced the teacher. The central move is to make coaching evidence-led and collaborative: prompt the teacher to name their own strengths, test a hypothesis with objective data, then co-script and rehearse one specific next step.
points: Specific, evidence-backed praise, limited to about three items and delivered as a prompt for the teacher to explain why they did it, builds awareness as well as goodwill.
Framing a weakness as a testable hypothesis, and being prepared to drop it if the evidence refutes it, keeps the observer honest.
Objective critical evidence such as photos, timings, audio and quotes is what lets a teacher accept an issue without a gotcha moment.
Diagnostic questions gauge the strength of the teacher's mental model, which determines how directive the coaching needs to be.
The suggested action should be one specific, rehearsed step for an upcoming lesson, co-scripted so that responsibility is shared and the stakes are low.
quotes: I don’t write down things like: I liked your questioning. Instead, it is: I liked the question you asked Isaac about the first step when factorising a quadratic. The more specific, the more meaningful, and if supported by evidence such as a photo or a quote, even better.

So, I describe the action they did that I liked - such as the question to Isaac about factorising quadratics - but then ask them to tell me why they did it. This serves two purposes: It gives me better insight into how aware they are of their strengths and what effective teaching looks like, and it makes the praise more potent if they can identify it themselves.

I hope my evidence-gathering leads me to the conclusion that my hypothesis is wrong, because that means that students are learning more than I feared. If my hypothesis is wrong then - despite my belief that the teacher could do something better - I must ditch it and form a new hypothesis.
With some clear, objective critical evidence, presented sensitively, however, most teachers jump on board and are ready to embrace making a change to their practice.

But this is not a gotcha moment where I reveal how smart I am and how foolish the teacher is. I said I thought it might be a bit more than that, and so I tested it by taking some photos of the boards of the students on the back row.

Plan the step together. Co-script precisely what the teacher will say and do. This helps with buy-in, improves the chances of success, and also reduces the stakes for the teacher due to the shared responsibility.

Rehearsal allows you, as a coach, to see if the teacher has understood what has been discussed. It also allows the teacher to try out the idea in a low-stakes environment with the opportunity for immediate feedback, as opposed to in the carnage of a lesson under the gaze of 30 pairs of eyes.
